newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Paris air show leaves questions unanswered.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Paris air show leaves questions unanswered.

text.p: European aerospace executives, weary from a week of glad-handing fellow professionals and the roar of fighter jets overhead, were left pondering the shape of things to come as the 42nd Paris air show closed on Sunday.

There were more questions than answers after newly-elected French Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin gave the traditional industry address on Saturday, raising but not addressing the issues of industry consolidation.

European and U.S. executives wanted to know the government's plans for defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF and whether a merger between state-owned Aerospatiale and privately-owned Dassault Aviation would go ahead.

Jospin would only say the government would be guided by the national interest in deciding Thomson-CSF's fate and nothing was ruled out. On the Dassault/Aerospatiale merger, he thought it was essential to bring civil and military capabilities together.
He gave no flight map for the route ahead.

But then, as the Communist transport minister Jean-Claude Gayssot told air show reporters earlier in the week: "I have an advantage and a disadvantage -- I am new in this job. I am studying and consulting".
U.S., British and German executives believe privatisation must take place to allow industry consolidation.

Gayssot was side-stepping a question on when France would privatise Aerospatiale, a move viewed by private firms British Aerospace Plc (BAe) and Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (Dasa) as vital to changing the Airbus Industrie consortium into a limited company.
That corporate change is seen as a decisive step in rationalising European commercial aircraft production and paving the way for military integration across borders.
Air shows are notorious for egging on the ultra-competitive instincts of this money-driven industry, but usually the rivalry is between traditional foes, such as Airbus versus Boeing.

This time, a simmering feud between Airbus partners broke into the open, with BAe and Dasa copying letters sent to Aerospatiale to their industry ministers, spelling out that they want the future Airbus company to control its own assets.
News of the letters was leaked. That was seen as a public rebuke to Aerospatiale, which is keen to hang on to its crown jewel, the design office, rather than vest it in the new Airbus.

But while the bickering went on, Airbus managing director Jean Pierson was sending a Mayday distress signal to the industry and anti-trust authorities over what he saw as the threat to kill off Airbus from a pending merger between U.S. giants Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas.
Previous air shows have seen a ritual trading of jibes between Airbus and Boeing over market shares and product performance. But this time, the game got serious.
The Boeing-McDonnell merger will create a group with $48 billion in annual sales, spanning civil, military and space actitivies.
Airbus, which had revenues of $8.8 billion in 1996, sees the merger as aimed at killing it off eventually.
Pierson also attacked Boeing's exclusive supply agreements with AMR Corp's American Airlines, Continental Airlines and Delta Air Lines, which lock out the European grouping for more than 20 years.
Boeing said the supply deals had nothing to do with the merger and the airlines themselves asked for the terms.

Boeing Commercial Airplane Group president Ron Woodard said an exclusive CFM56 engine agreement on its bestselling 737 jet supported 11,000 French jobs and the Next Generation 737 would bring in $6.8 billion in revenues for France's state-owned Snecma engine firm.
Airbus does not have the luxury of time before the benefits of the Boeing/McDonnell merger start showing in a couple of years and bear down on the European venture, analysts said.

Airbus' status change is also tied to a strategic product, the 500-seater A3XX, which it badly needs to attack Boeing's 747 monopoly at the high capacity end. Airbus needs equity partners for the A3XX but it is not clear firms want to take part while it remains shackled with its present cumbersome organisation, they said.

Airbus, under pressure to get a quick-fix solution to Boeing's Jumbo, launched the A340-500 and A340-600 derivatives of its long-range, four-engine jet at the air show. It also announced it would be selling an A319 derivative as its Corporate Jet offering, to rival the Boeing Business Jet niche product.
The A340-600 will seat 378 passengers, taking it close to the 400 flown on the 747, which is Boeing's high-margin product.

But elsewhere, hopes for a launch of a new AirJet 70 regional jet from the AI(R) marketing consortium were left grounded, as a decision was postponed. The $1.4 billion AirJet project was seen as competing with a 100-seater Asian Express which Airbus will build with China, South Korea and Singapore.
The regional jet market got a lift with U.S. airline orders for newly-launched products.

Brazil's Embraer soared, with orders from Continental Express and American Eagle. The Continental order will launch a long-range version of its EMB-145 jet, worth around $350 million, while American Eagle is buying 42 of the shorter-range version, worth $700 million.
American Eagle, an AMR unit, became the launch customer for Bombardier's 70-seat Canadair CRJ 700, with an order for 25 aircraft worth $700 million.

In the ailing military market, where the peace dividend has forced meant declining sales and factory closures, BAe ended months of speculation by teaming up with Lockheed Martin's bid to build the U.S. Joint Strike Fighter (JSF).

Lockheed is competing against Boeing for the JSF, which is the Pentagon's attempt to build a common aircraft for all its armed services and save billions of taxpayer dollars. The prize is to build 3,000 planes with a target price tag of $30 million each. The British navy expects to order 60 JSF aircraft.
While the U.S. fighter for the 21st century picked up speed, the four-nation Eurofighter was left dangling for funds.

Germany's cash-strapped government has to vote funds for the Eurofighter by the end of July, or Dasa will stop pre-production work, Dasa chief executive Manfred Bischoff said. But he said he was optimistic the funds would be found.
Trade union officials from Britain, Germany, Italy and Spain warned 50,000 jobs were on the line.

Airbus announced it had won $3.5 billion of business at the air show, but the bulk of that was made up of a memorandum of understanding from U.S. carrier Northwest Airlines, rather than a firm order, worth $2 billion for 50 A319s.
Boeing responded later in the week with an order from British Airways Plc, worth around $1 billion, for five 777 giant twinjets and three 767 wide-body twins.
With the serious business on hand of restructuring Airbus, and with Boeing facing a European Commission anti-trust probe on its merger, the game of chase for orders had lost some of its fizz.
The next Paris air show is June 1999, when the shape of the new Airbus should be close to completion, ready for competiton in the next century.
